source: OSF preprint (2017) Cognition and the self: independent close replication of self-construal priming on spatial memory (Kuhnen and Oyserman 2002, Study 2)
finding: Pre-registered, close, digital replication of the pronoun-click prime followed by a spatial grid memory task, in Waterloo students. It is the only large Western-sample pre-registered replication of a pronoun-task prime I could open.
numbers: Target 130 per condition. 244 completed; 240 after removing nonsense answers and technical problems; 47 more removed for self-reported inattention. Compliance = share of 20 pronouns clicked. Full compliance N=87 (43 independent, 44 interdependent); partial (>75%) N=154 to 157 (text and table differ); no filter N=193 (98 and 95).
limits: Pronoun clicking replaced circling. Authors admit they did not pre-register the compliance cut-off. Part of a three-study package, so fatigue is possible.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 4: the pronoun prime does work in a Western sample, but only among people who did the prime task.

source: OSF preprint (2017) Cognition and the self: independent close replication of self-construal priming on spatial memory (Kuhnen and Oyserman 2002, Study 2) - Table 1
finding: Effect size falls as the compliance filter loosens. The interdependent prime gave better recall than the independent prime only among full compliers.
numbers: Full compliance N=87: object recall 44.60 vs 54.38 percent, t(84.93)=2.31, p=.028, d=.50; location recall d=.52 (p=.024); object-and-location d=.47 (p=.031). Partial N=157: d=.26, .30, .29 (p=.108, .073, .080). No filter N=193: d=.10, .15, .15 (all p>.25).
limits: Filtering on post-treatment behaviour breaks randomisation; compliers may differ. Exploratory, not pre-registered.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a compliance gate matters. For an LLM, check the cue was followed before crediting it. The effect among followers was 3 to 5 times the unfiltered effect.

source: OSF preprint (2017) Cognition and the self: independent close replication of self-construal priming on spatial memory (Kuhnen and Oyserman 2002, Study 2) - effect size context and ethnic group
finding: Pooling this study with earlier close and conceptual replications of Kuhnen and Oyserman Study 2 gives a small effect. Drouin and Davidson (2015, JEP General, four experiments, Canadian students) found effects smaller than the original. Prime effect and ethnic-group effect were largely independent.
numbers: Average d=.32, median d=.34 across conceptual and close replications; average d=.35, median d=.37 for close replications only, from only three independent labs. White vs non-white object recall at full compliance F(1,82)=6.39, p=.013, d=.56.
limits: Authors say a multi-lab replication is still needed. I found no Many Labs run of pronoun circling or SDFF.
agent_relevance: Use d about .3 as the prior for cue gain. Gap 4 stays partly open: no multi-lab replication.

source: OSF preprint (2017) Cognition and the self: independent close replication of self-construal priming on spatial memory (Kuhnen and Oyserman 2002, Study 2) - authors' reading of the null
finding: Authors argue the effect depends on how many non-compliers enter the analysis. They also show the effect is not specific to object-in-location memory, which weakens the original mechanism claim.
numbers: Adding back participants who said they were inattentive made full-compliance object and object-location effects marginal (t(105.87)=1.88, p=.063; t(104.97)=1.96, p=.052).
quote: replicability of the effect ... hinges on the degree to which non-compliant participants are included in analyses
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the human null reads as a weak, dose-dependent prime, not a fixed trait. For LLM cues, vary cue strength and check a monotone response.

source: Lu, Song and Zhang (2025) Cultural tendencies in generative AI. Nature Human Behaviour 10.1038/s41562-025-02242-1
finding: Abstract only (full text behind subscription; Europe PMC lists it as not open access). GPT in Chinese is more interdependent and holistic than in English; the same for ERNIE. Exploratory cultural prompts (assume the role of a Chinese person) shift these tendencies.
numbers: No effect sizes, item counts or prompt text were reachable.
limits: Paywalled. The abstract itself calls the prompt analyses exploratory.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: persona-cue replication on many items and current models has no source in hand.

source: Yang, Hechtbauer, Khalilov, Brinkmann, Schmitt and Feldhus (2026) Persona Prompting as a Lens on LLM Social Reasoning. EACL 2026
finding: Persona prompting raised hate-speech classification accuracy but lowered rationale quality. Simulated personas did not match real demographic groups; high agreement between personas suggests the models resist steering.
numbers: Abstract only; three LLMs; no metrics on the page.
limits: Task is hate speech, not holistic-analytic reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a persona can raise the label score and still weaken the reasoning. Check the reasoning, not only the answer.

source: Lee et al. (2024) Persona is a double-edged sword: Jekyll and Hyde (arXiv 2408.08631) - confusion matrices
finding: Within one model, a persona flips about as many items to wrong as to right. This is the item-level version of the 19-29 percent backfire seen with country cues.
numbers: AQuA: wrong-to-right with persona 15.75 percent of items, right-to-wrong 13.78 percent (both right 37.40, both wrong 33.07). Coin Flip: 4.00 percent gained, 18.00 percent lost (both right 73.40).
limits: Role-play personas, not culture cues. One model run shown in Table 1.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a near-zero net cue effect can hide large per-item gains and losses, so a revert step has room to work.

source: Lee et al. (2024) Persona is a double-edged sword: Jekyll and Hyde (arXiv 2408.08631) - arithmetic table
finding: On six arithmetic sets persona helps on average, and a step that compares persona and neutral answers with a position-bias-free LLM judge helps more. This is the nearest tested analogue of compare-to-reference and revert-if-worse.
numbers: Average accuracy: GPT-4 base 91.06, persona 92.28, Jekyll and Hyde 93.15. GPT-3.5-turbo 84.78, 86.45, 87.71. llama3-8B 81.47, 82.32, 84.23. Three runs averaged. AQuA GPT-4 68.24, 74.80, 76.90.
limits: Judge is the same LLM and needs several extra calls per verdict, so not equal compute. Personas are roles like math teacher, not culture.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 answered in kind: choosing between cued and neutral output beat either alone by about 1 to 2 points on average. No culture test.

source: Lee et al. (2024) Persona is a double-edged sword: Jekyll and Hyde (arXiv 2408.08631) - common sense, symbolic and other tasks
finding: Persona can hurt on some tasks and models; the select-better step recovers part of the loss. The big Coin Flip and Letter gains from persona look like a reasoning trigger rather than a role effect.
numbers: llama3-8B: CSQA base 74.50, persona 72.29, J and H 74.97; Date 77.42, 74.44, 79.04; average 74.68, 74.49, 76.38. GPT-4 Coin Flip 66.93, 75.93, 80.27; Letter 19.80, 92.80, 93.00; Strategy 76.42, 75.71, 77.00. Abstract: persona degraded reasoning in 7 of 12 datasets on llama3.
limits: Letter and Coin are symbolic tasks where the step-by-step format matters; the GPT-4 baseline there is very low.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the sign of a persona cue differs by model and task (GPT-4 up, llama3 flat or down). Any orientation cue needs a per-model, per-task panel.

source: Kong et al. (2023) Better zero-shot reasoning with role-play prompting (arXiv 2308.07702)
finding: Role-play prompting beat plain zero-shot on most of 12 reasoning benchmarks with ChatGPT.
numbers: AQuA 53.5 to 63.8 percent; Last Letter 23.8 to 84.2 percent (abstract figures).
limits: Abstract page only. Baseline was plain zero-shot, not a neutral prefix of equal length.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: closest to a prefix test, but a role cue that sets up chain-of-thought is confounded with extra reasoning tokens.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee and Jurgens (2023) When a helpful assistant is not really helpful: personas in system prompts (arXiv 2311.10054)
finding: Adding a persona to the system prompt did not improve accuracy over no persona. Persona type, gender and domain still shifted accuracy, and choosing the best persona automatically was about as good as random.
numbers: 162 roles, 6 relationship types, 8 expertise domains, 4 LLM families, 2,410 factual questions.
limits: Factual questions, not holistic-analytic items. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: in prefix tests of this kind the average cue effect on accuracy is about zero. Expect the same for orientation cues unless the item is style-sensitive.

source: Hu and Collier (2024) Quantifying the persona effect in LLM simulations (arXiv 2402.10811)
finding: Persona variables explain under 10 percent of variance in human annotations. Persona prompting gives modest but significant gains, mostly on items where annotators disagree mildly.
numbers: Zero-shot 70B model with persona captures 81 percent of what a linear regression on true labels gets.
agent_relevance: Gap 9/10: cue effect is bounded by how much the cue variable predicts the target. Cues help on ambiguous items, not fixed ones.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (arXiv 2310.13548)
finding: Five assistants show sycophancy across four free-form tasks. Responses matching a user's views are preferred by humans and preference models, even over correct ones.
limits: Abstract only. User views, not a claimed cultural identity.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: gives a mechanism for persona-cue gains (agree with the claimed identity). Direct test (same cue with and without an identity claim) not found in any source.

source: Training language models to be warm can reduce accuracy and increase sycophancy. Nature 2026 (10.1038/s41586-026-10410-0)
finding: Training for warmth raised error rates and validation of wrong user beliefs, most when users expressed sadness, across five models, while standard tests stayed unchanged.
numbers: +10 to +30 percentage points more errors than the original models (Crossref abstract).
limits: Fine-tuning, not prompting. Abstract via Crossref only.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a social-style cue can raise agreement with the user at a cost to accuracy, and standard benchmarks may not show it.

source: Cultural Norm-based Cultural Alignment: Reasoning Shapes Alignment (AAAI 2026, 10.1609/aaai.v40i21.38839)
finding: Putting mined cultural norms into context improves cultural alignment, and models with stronger reasoning gain more.
limits: Abstract only (publisher page blocked). Survey alignment, not reasoning style.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: cue gain may depend on model capacity, not only baseline style. A content cue with norms beats a bare label.

source: Cultural Value Alignment in LLMs: Schwartz values in Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek (OSF preprint 2025)
finding: Baselines differ by model: all emphasise self-transcendence; DeepSeek alone downplayed self-enhancement values relative to ChatGPT and Gemini.
numbers: 40-item Portrait Values Questionnaire; Bayesian ordinal regression. No cue tested.
limits: No priming or cue; no Claude.
agent_relevance: Gap 6/9: baseline orientation differs between vendors, so run a fixed cue panel per model and measure the baseline first.

source: Search note, gap pass (2026-11): no study found on equal-token prefix cues, task-structure vs culture-label cues, identity-free vs persona cues, or accessibility-times-applicability models of LLM priming
finding: About 12 Crossref queries on self-construal and LLMs, priming accessibility in LLMs, sycophancy to identity, and cultural prompting across Claude, Gemini and open models returned no paper that tests these. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited and the WebSearch budget was spent, so absence is weak evidence.
numbers: About 12 queries, 6 to 7 results each, none on point.
limits: Thin search; Nature paper text and the full Lu et al. paper were not reachable.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 8 (direct test) and 10 stay open: they are experiments to run, not literature to find.
